articles.title: Agentic search over a hierarchy of document clusters
articles.excerpt: To run agentic search over a hierarchy of document clusters, first cluster the corpus: embed every document, then split the embeddings recursively into a tree, and give each cluster a label and a shor…
articles.body: To run agentic search over a hierarchy of document clusters, first cluster the corpus: embed every document, then split the embeddings recursively into a tree, and give each cluster a label and a short summary. At query time an agent navigates the tree top-down. It reads the summaries at one level, chooses which clusters to open, descends into them, and runs vector or keyword search only inside the chosen leaf clusters. It stops when the evidence it has gathered answers the question. The agent never sees the whole corpus, only the summaries on its path and the chunks from a few leaves. The rest of this post covers why that works, how to build the tree, what the loop looks like in code, and where it fails.
articles.author: Ethan Steininger

articles.title: Is There a Reverse Video Search? How It Works, How to Build One
articles.excerpt: Yes. Reverse video search exists, but the big search engines do not offer it as a single upload box. The usual workflow is to pull keyframes out of the video and run each one through a reverse image s…
articles.body: Yes. Reverse video search exists, but the big search engines do not offer it as a single upload box. The usual workflow is to pull keyframes out of the video and run each one through a reverse image search. Under the hood, a dedicated system does the same thing at scale: it samples frames or detects shot boundaries, turns each frame into a perceptual hash or an embedding, stores them in an index, and matches the frames of your query clip against that index. The best-matching frames also carry timestamps, so the answer comes back as "this file, at 01:42". Consumer tools search the public web's image index. If you want to search a video library you own, you build or buy the index yourself. Consumer options Google Lens.

articles.body: Short answer: For a text summarization API cost comparison in Node.js, choose the model that clears your quality and latency gates at the lowest measured accepted cost, then recheck the result against the real gaming report mix. A gaming moderation queue needs a short, faithful summary quickly; a cheap model that drops the target, threat, or evidence creates review work and can increase latency through retries. The comparison is about the whole workflow, not a headline token price. I would route reports through a small evaluation harness, keep the model behind a provider-neutral interface, and record input tokens, output tokens, elapsed time, retry count, and reviewer outcome for every sample. The result is a decision rule you can defend.

articles.title: Designing a URL Shortener: My First High-Level System Design
articles.excerpt: Exploring API design, Redis caching, database capacity, horizontal scaling, and asynchronous analytics. System design has always seemed like one of those skills that becomes easier only when you start…
articles.body: Exploring API design, Redis caching, database capacity, horizontal scaling, and asynchronous analytics. System design has always seemed like one of those skills that becomes easier only when you start building systems on paper. So, I decided to start practicing High-Level Design (HLD) by designing a familiar application: a URL shortener. At first glance, a URL shortener looks simple. You provide a long URL, receive a short link, and redirect users when they visit it. But what happens when millions of users create links and billions of redirects need to be processed? How do we keep redirects fast? How do we handle traffic spikes? And how do we collect analytics without slowing down the redirect path?

articles.title: I Taught a Local Gemma to Clean My Downloads Folder, Offline
articles.excerpt: What I Built My Downloads folder is a landfill. IMG_4821.heic, final_v3.docx, a LICENSE with no context, installers from months ago. Every few weeks I promise myself I'll sort it, and every few weeks…
articles.body: What I Built My Downloads folder is a landfill. IMG_4821.heic , final_v3.docx , a LICENSE with no context, installers from months ago. Every few weeks I promise myself I'll sort it, and every few weeks I don't. So I built lazy-tidy : a tiny Python script that sorts a messy folder into Documents , Images , Videos , Audio , Code , Archives , Installers and Other . It previews by default and only moves files when I pass --apply . The "slow and steady" part: it uses the cheapest decision-maker first. Known extensions are sorted instantly with a lookup table. Only files the table can't place ( Makefile , README , data.bin , photo.raw ) are handed to a local open-weight model, Gemma 3 4B running through Ollama on my laptop.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.
